title: What is an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) and a technical RFC — an ADR documents a specific architecture decision (context/problem, decision made, consequences, alternatives considered) while an RFC is a broader proposal for a significant change seeking feedback before commitment — why should both be version-controlled alongside the code (decisions are traceable, new team members understand WHY things are the way they are, prevents re-debating settled decisions), and what makes a good ADR (concise context, clear decision, honest trade-offs)?
shortTitle: Architecture Decision Records (ADR) and technical RFCs — what they are and why version-control them
topicTitle: What is an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) and a technical RFC

s1_definition.profdef: An Architecture Decision Record, or ADR, is a short document that captures one significant architecture decision — the context and problem, the decision made, the alternatives considered, and the consequences. A technical RFC, Request for Comments, is a broader proposal document that describes a significant proposed change and circulates for feedback before the team commits. Both are written in plain text like Markdown and stored in version control alongside the code so decisions are traceable, newcomers understand why things are the way they are, and settled questions are not re-litigated.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India decides to switch its core settlement from overnight batch to real-time. An RFC is the detailed proposal circulated to all departments beforehand — here is what we want to change, why, the options, the risks — inviting everyone to comment before any commitment. An ADR is the official minute recorded once a specific decision is made — we chose real-time settlement over batch on this date, for these reasons, with these trade-offs. Keeping both in the same filing system as the operational manuals means a new manager years later can open the file and understand exactly why the bank works the way it does, instead of reopening a debate everyone already had.
s1_definition.oneliner: An ADR records one settled decision with its trade-offs; an RFC proposes a bigger change for feedback first; version-controlling both makes decisions traceable and stops endless re-debate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An Architecture Decision Record, or ADR, is a short document that captures one significant architecture decision — the context and problem, the decision made, the alternatives considered, and the consequences. A technical RFC, Request for Comments, is a broader proposal document that describes a significant proposed change and circulates for feedback before the team commits. Both are written in plain text like Markdown and stored in version control alongside the code so decisions are traceable, newcomers understand why things are the way they are, and settled questions are not re-litigated.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India decides to switch its core settlement from overnight batch to real-time. An RFC is the detailed proposal circulated to all departments beforehand — here is what we want to change, why, the options, the risks — inviting everyone to comment before any commitment. An ADR is the official minute recorded once a specific decision is made — we chose real-time settlement over batch on this date, for these reasons, with these trade-offs. Keeping both in the same filing system as the operational manuals means a new manager years later can open the file and understand exactly why the bank works the way it does, instead of reopening a debate everyone already had.

**One line to remember:** An ADR records one settled decision with its trade-offs; an RFC proposes a bigger change for feedback first; version-controlling both makes decisions traceable and stops endless re-debate.

sections.s2_technical:
An ADR documents a single architecture decision in a consistent, lightweight format. The typical sections are: a title and a status such as proposed, accepted, or superseded; the context, which states the problem and the forces at play; the decision, which states clearly what was chosen; the alternatives considered, which lists the other options and why they were not chosen; and the consequences, which honestly describes what becomes easier and what becomes harder as a result. ADRs are deliberately short — often one page — because their value is in being written at all and being easy to read later. They are numbered and append-only: you do not rewrite an old ADR, you add a new one that supersedes it, preserving the historical record of how thinking evolved.

A technical RFC is broader and comes earlier in the process. Where an ADR records a decision that has been made, an RFC proposes a significant change and seeks feedback before commitment. It describes the motivation, the detailed design, the alternatives, the risks and the migration path, and then circulates to stakeholders who comment, question, and suggest improvements. After discussion, the team either adopts the proposal — often recording the final decision as an ADR — or rejects it. RFCs suit larger, cross-cutting changes like adopting a new messaging platform or changing an authentication model, where many people's input is needed before committing.

Why version-control both alongside the code is the heart of the question. First, traceability: when the documents live in the same repository as the code and go through the same pull-request process, every decision has a date, an author, reviewers, and a history, which is exactly what auditors in a bank require. Second, onboarding: a new engineer can read the ADRs and understand why the system is shaped the way it is — why we chose this database, why we settle on T plus one, why we avoided a particular framework — without having to interrupt senior colleagues or guess. Third, and this is underrated, it prevents re-debating settled decisions: when someone asks months later "why don't we just use X," the answer is a link to the ADR that already weighed X and explained the trade-off, so the team does not burn hours relitigating a closed question. Keeping the docs next to the code also means they evolve with the code and are reviewed with the same rigor, rather than rotting in a wiki nobody updates.

What makes a good ADR is concision, clarity, and honesty. Concise context: state the problem and the real constraints in a few sentences, not pages. A clear, unambiguous decision: a reader should know exactly what was decided without interpretation. And honest trade-offs: a good ADR does not pretend the choice is perfect; it states plainly what you give up. For a bank, that honesty is valuable because it documents known risks — if we chose eventual consistency for performance, the ADR says so, and when a related issue surfaces later, the team already understands the deliberate trade-off rather than treating it as a surprise bug. A senior-level nuance I always mention: the discipline is not bureaucracy for its own sake; it is cheap insurance. Writing a one-page ADR takes twenty minutes and saves days of future confusion and repeated arguments, and in a regulated industry it is often part of demonstrating sound governance.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's settlement team must decide how to make trade settlement more timely and wants the decision properly recorded.

Problem 1 — six months ago the team informally chose a message queue, but nobody wrote down why, and now a new engineer keeps asking "why not just use direct REST calls." This is exactly what an ADR prevents — a recorded decision with its trade-offs stops the question from reopening endlessly.

Problem 2 — the proposed shift from overnight batch to near-real-time settlement is a big, cross-cutting change touching many teams. This is exactly what an RFC is for — circulate the proposal for feedback and risk review before committing.

Problem 3 — auditors ask for evidence of how and when the settlement architecture decision was made and who approved it. This is exactly why the documents live in version control — the git history and pull request supply the date, author, reviewers, and rationale.

The mini-project is a real ADR file and a real RFC file stored in the repository next to the code, plus a small SettlementPublisher Java class that reflects the decided design. We show how they are reviewed through a pull request like code.

sections.s4d_java:
```markdown
<!-- File: docs/adr/0007-use-kafka-for-settlement-events.md -->
# 7. Use Kafka for settlement events

Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-04-12
Deciders: settlement-team, platform-architecture

## Context
Settlement must notify downstream services (audit, notification, reporting)
when a trade settles. These consumers must be decoupled from the settlement
write path, and we must not lose events if a consumer is temporarily down.
Volume is up to 50,000 settlements per day with bursts at market close.

## Decision
We will publish settlement events to a Kafka topic. Settlement writes to the
database and publishes an event; consumers subscribe independently.

## Alternatives considered
- Direct synchronous REST calls to each consumer: rejected because settlement
  would block on slow consumers and lose events if a consumer is down.
- A database polling table: rejected due to added latency and DB load.

## Consequences
- Easier: new consumers subscribe without changing settlement; durable, replayable.
- Harder: we now operate a Kafka cluster and must handle eventual consistency
  and consumer idempotency. This trade-off is accepted deliberately.
```

```markdown
<!-- File: docs/adr/0008-adopt-near-real-time-settlement.md -->
# 8. Adopt near-real-time settlement (supersedes batch)

Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-10-20
Supersedes: (the earlier informal "overnight batch" approach)
Related RFC: docs/rfc/0003-near-real-time-settlement.md

## Context
Overnight batch settlement delays confirmations by up to a day, hurting
customer experience and regulatory reporting timeliness.

## Decision
Settle trades near-real-time via the existing Kafka event pipeline (see ADR 7),
processing each settlement within seconds instead of a nightly batch.

## Alternatives considered
- Keep overnight batch: rejected; too slow for current requirements.
- Full synchronous settlement in the request path: rejected; latency + coupling.

## Consequences
- Easier: faster confirmations, timelier reporting.
- Harder: higher operational complexity, needs robust monitoring and back-pressure
  handling at market close. Accepted with a monitoring plan.
```

```markdown
<!-- File: docs/rfc/0003-near-real-time-settlement.md -->
# RFC 3: Near-real-time settlement

Status: Under review
Author: r.kumar
Reviewers: settlement-team, platform-architecture, compliance

## Motivation
Overnight batch settlement is too slow for customer and regulatory needs.
This RFC proposes moving to near-real-time settlement and seeks feedback
BEFORE we commit.

## Proposed design
Reuse the Kafka pipeline from ADR 7. A SettlementPublisher emits an event per
settled trade; a consumer updates ledgers and triggers confirmations within
seconds. Include idempotency keys to avoid double-processing on retries.

## Alternatives
- Micro-batches every 5 minutes (simpler, but still delayed).
- Synchronous settlement (lowest latency, highest coupling and risk).

## Risks & migration
- Market-close bursts: mitigate with partitioning and back-pressure.
- Migration: run batch and real-time in parallel for two weeks, reconcile daily.

## Open questions
- Do we need exactly-once semantics, or is at-least-once + idempotency enough?

<!-- After review, the agreed outcome is recorded as ADR 0008. -->
```

```java
// ─── File: src/main/java/com/bank/settlement/SettlementPublisher.java ───
package com.bank.settlement;

import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

// Code reflects ADR 7 (Kafka events) and ADR 8 (near-real-time). The ADRs
// explain WHY this uses Kafka rather than REST — a newcomer reads them first.
@Component
public class SettlementPublisher {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    public SettlementPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka) {
        this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    // Publish a settlement event near-real-time with an idempotency key,
    // exactly as the RFC proposed and ADR 8 accepted.
    public void publishSettled(String tradeId, String accountId, BigDecimal amount) {
        String key = tradeId;   // idempotency: consumers dedupe on tradeId
        String event = String.format(
                "{\"tradeId\":\"%s\",\"accountId\":\"%s\",\"amount\":\"%s\",\"status\":\"SETTLED\"}",
                tradeId, accountId, amount);
        kafka.send("trade.settled", key, event);
    }
}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# ADRs and RFCs are reviewed like code — through a pull request.
git checkout -b docs/adr-0008-real-time-settlement
git add docs/adr/0008-adopt-near-real-time-settlement.md
git commit -m "ADR-0008 adopt near-real-time settlement (supersedes batch)"
git push -u origin docs/adr-0008-real-time-settlement
# Open a PR: reviewers comment on the decision; merge records it with history.

# Trace WHEN and WHY a decision was made (audit evidence):
git log --oneline -- docs/adr/0008-adopt-near-real-time-settlement.md

# Find the decision that answers "why Kafka not REST?"
grep -rl "Kafka" docs/adr/

# Build the service whose design the ADRs document.
mvn clean package
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the settlement team wants to move from overnight batch to near-real-time settlement and must propose, decide, and record it properly.

Step 1: An engineer writes RFC 3, describing the motivation, the proposed Kafka-based design, the alternatives, the risks, and open questions, and opens it as a pull request so the whole team and compliance can comment before anything is committed.

Step 2: Reviewers add comments — compliance asks about reconciliation during migration, and a platform engineer questions whether exactly-once is needed. The RFC is updated to answer these, exactly the feedback loop an RFC is designed to provide before commitment.

Step 3: The team reaches agreement. The RFC's outcome is crystallized into ADR 8, a short record stating the decision to adopt near-real-time settlement, the alternatives rejected, and the honest trade-off of higher operational complexity.

Step 4: ADR 8 is opened as its own pull request, reviewed, and merged. Because it lives in version control, the merge stamps it with a date, author, and reviewers — the audit evidence of how and when the decision was made.

Step 5: Months later a new engineer asks why settlement uses Kafka instead of direct REST calls. Instead of a meeting, a teammate links ADR 7, which already weighed REST and explained why it was rejected. The settled decision is not re-debated.

Step 6: The SettlementPublisher code is built to match ADR 7 and ADR 8, and because the docs sit beside the code and are reviewed the same way, they stay accurate as the system evolves rather than rotting in a forgotten wiki.

sections.s6_takeaway:
An Architecture Decision Record, or ADR, is a short document that captures one significant architecture decision. It has a consistent structure: the context stating the problem and the forces at play, the decision stating clearly what was chosen, the alternatives considered with why they were rejected, and the consequences honestly describing what becomes easier and what becomes harder. ADRs are deliberately brief — often a page — numbered, and append-only, so you never rewrite an old one; you add a new one that supersedes it, preserving how the thinking evolved.

A technical RFC, Request for Comments, is broader and comes earlier. Where an ADR records a decision already made, an RFC proposes a significant change and seeks feedback before commitment. It lays out the motivation, the detailed design, the alternatives, the risks, and the migration path, then circulates to stakeholders who comment and question. After discussion the team adopts it — often recording the final decision as an ADR — or rejects it. RFCs suit large, cross-cutting changes where many people's input is needed first.

I version-control both alongside the code for three reasons. Traceability: because they live in the repository and go through the same pull-request process, every decision has a date, an author, and reviewers, which is exactly what auditors in a bank require. Onboarding: a new engineer can read the ADRs and understand why the system is shaped the way it is without interrupting senior colleagues. And preventing re-debate: when someone asks months later why we did not just use some alternative, the answer is a link to the ADR that already weighed it, so the team does not burn hours relitigating a closed question. Keeping the docs beside the code also means they are reviewed with the same rigor and stay accurate instead of rotting in a wiki.

What makes a good ADR is concision, clarity, and honesty — a brief context, an unambiguous decision, and trade-offs stated plainly rather than pretending the choice is perfect. At National Bank of India, when we moved settlement from overnight batch to near-real-time, we circulated an RFC for the big cross-cutting proposal, gathered feedback from compliance and platform, and then recorded the outcome as an ADR that honestly noted the higher operational complexity we accepted. When a new engineer later asked why settlement uses Kafka rather than REST, we simply linked the earlier ADR that had already weighed that exact trade-off. The discipline is not bureaucracy; it is cheap insurance — a twenty-minute document that saves days of future confusion and, in a regulated industry, demonstrates sound governance.
